prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Except when once we drew identical lots nothing’s ever come between us. We keep our drifts of space spare and daily shake our down. You’ve glanced beyond your dirty cuffs and caught me hand-washing my clean shirts. Stuck with sharp wind, both bloods are rare and rarely do we taste the walnut’s knot of oil. We wake between our fitted sheets and shake our fists or pretend real fright but not in this do we dare touch. My rib cage can stand in yours, yours become the swinging doors through which magician’s swords will slice and miss that knotted muscle. It is a trick. We’ll make an endless show of the outright clanking, irregular beating of our acrobatic hearts. We’ve designed the double bars of depth; our hearts skip — the tumbleset we think is absence, the somersault we call forbearance — the hearts are there, doing turns that teach us to count and keep each finger close to its own sly pulse.

outputs.L1: Save for the one occasion we drew matching lots, nothing has ever truly come between us. We keep our expanses of space sparing, shaking off each day's accumulation like settling down. You have glanced past your own soiled cuffs to catch me hand-washing shirts already clean. Bound together by a biting wind, we are both of rare blood, and rarer still do we taste the walnut's knot of oil. We wake beneath our fitted sheets, shaking our fists or feigning genuine fright—yet in this alone we dare not touch. My rib cage might stand within yours, and yours become the swinging doors through which a magician's swords will slice and miss that knotted muscle. It is all artifice. We stage an endless performance of the clattering, irregular beat of our acrobatic hearts. We have built the double bars of depth; our hearts falter—the tumble we mistake for absence, the somersault we call forbearance—yet the hearts remain, turning and turning, teaching us to count, keeping each finger close to its own furtive pulse.
outputs.L2: Aside from that single occasion when fate paired us by chance, nothing has managed to separate us. The distance between us stays minimal, and each day we shed what has settled on us. You've seen through the grime on your own sleeves to notice me scrubbing my shirts until they're spotless. Battered by a harsh breeze, we share the rarity of our blood types, and only occasionally do we savor the richness of walnut oil. Rising together beneath sheets pulled tight, we might clench our fists or feign terror, yet neither of us risks actual contact in these moments. My chest cavity could nest within yours, and your ribs might become gates that a magician's blades pass through, narrowly missing that tangled muscle we call a heart. It's all illusion. Endlessly we perform this spectacle—the jarring, uneven rhythm of our daring hearts. We've constructed layered barriers of distance; our heartbeats stutter—what seems like a tumble we interpret as separation, what seems like a flip we call patience—yet the hearts remain, practicing maneuvers that teach us how to keep track, each finger attuned to its own secretive rhythm.
outputs.L3:
# On the Architecture of a Shared Life

Throughout the long arc of their relationship, the speakers have remained remarkably close—bound together in a way that only fate itself, appearing once as some identical and inescapable circumstance, has ever managed to interrupt. This singular disruption stands out precisely because of its rarity; otherwise, their proximity has been a constant, a given, the unquestioned backdrop against which everything else unfolds.

Yet this closeness does not mean transparency. They maintain careful, spare distances between them, adhering to daily routines that suggest order and predictability. And still, within this structured nearness, they catch glimpses of each other's quiet contradictions: dirty cuffs worn alongside shirts that have been washed by hand, kept meticulously clean. These small, telling details—the grime and the care existing side by side—reveal a complexity neither speaker fully articulates, evidence of lives that are simultaneously tended and neglected, presentable and frayed at the edges.

Their shared experience is marked by both rarity and fear, emotions that coexist without ever collapsing into the same thing. There is an unspoken boundary between them, a line neither dares to cross, and this restraint persists even in their most vulnerable, playful moments—waking together, shaking fists at each other in mock fright, performing fear as a kind of intimacy that stops short of something more genuine or dangerous.

This entwinement of identities creates space for a peculiar, dangerous magic: like a magician's trick, swords can slice perilously close to their hearts and yet, through some sleight of hand or fate, always miss the vital, knotted muscle beneath. The danger is real, but so is the impossible precision that keeps them both intact—wounded near-misses rather than fatal blows.

Over time, they have built an elaborate performance around emotional distance, mistaking their carefully maintained absence and quiet forbearance for something else entirely—imagining these gaps as the erratic, skipping rhythms of hearts caught mid-acrobatics, hearts that seem to falter or vanish. But in truth, these hearts have never actually left; they remain present, connected, beating steadily beneath the performance. And it is this very misunderstanding—this mistaking of restraint for absence—that has taught both speakers to guard their own pulse all the more closely, wary of a vulnerability they cannot quite name but sense is always near.
outputs.L4:
# Sword Box

We were born from the same cut,
you and I—two halves of one
astonished body, folded
into a single box
before the audience arrived.

They think this is a trick
of separation: the blade
sliding through the velvet walls,
missing you by inches,
missing me by less.

But watch closely—
we rehearsed this a thousand times
in the dark before we had names.
I know exactly where to bend
my spine away from steel
because I know exactly
where your spine begins.

This is not distance.
This is choreography.

Every sword that enters
the box and exits clean
is proof of how well
I have memorized your shape,
how perfectly you curl
around the absence of me
so that danger finds only air
where our hearts should collide.

People applaud the illusion—
gasp at how close
the blades come to skin,
how near the whole act teeters
toward disaster.

They do not see
that nearness is the point.
That what looks like almost-touching
is actually the tightest embrace
two bodies can perform
without becoming one wound.

We are acrobats of restraint,
somersaulting around
the shared organ we cannot name—
not quite heart, not quite hinge,
but the thing that keeps us
folding into each other's blind spots,
finding the exact pocket of safety
that only exists because
we built it together,
sword by sword,
box by box,
until the audience believes
we are two people
instead of one gesture
wearing two skins.

When the lid opens
and we both emerge unscathed,
they clap for the magic.

They do not understand
that the trick was never
about escaping the blade.

The trick was always
about how close
we could let it come
and still remain
intact—

still remain
each other's
only exit.
outputs.L5:
# Except You're Stuck

Everyone tells you to move forward. Look ahead. Let go of the past. It's good advice, really—the kind you'd give someone else without hesitation. Except you're stuck, and knowing the right direction doesn't mean you can walk it.

Being stuck isn't laziness, though it can look that way from the outside. It isn't a lack of desire to change, though people often assume that too. Sometimes it's fear wearing the mask of comfort. Sometimes it's grief that hasn't finished speaking. Sometimes it's simply that the mind and body haven't yet agreed to move in the same direction at the same time.

There's a particular loneliness in being stuck while everyone around you seems to be moving. Friends start new jobs, relationships, chapters. They ask how you're doing, and you say "fine," because the truth—*I haven't moved in months, not really*—feels too heavy for a casual conversation.

But here's something worth considering: being stuck is not the same as being broken. A stuck door isn't a broken door. Sometimes it just needs a different kind of push, or the humidity to change, or someone to notice it's swollen and plane down the edge that catches.

The mistake is believing that stuckness is a permanent address rather than a temporary weather pattern. You are not defined by this season. You are only *in* it.

So if you're stuck today, let that be true without turning it into a verdict on your worth. Feel the frustration without adding shame on top of it. The path forward will show itself, maybe not today, but it will. Until then, it's alright to simply stay where you are—stuck, yes, but still here, still breathing, still eventually going to move.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal free-verse poem about a strained sibling or twin relationship, using images of shared blood, distance, and hidden tenderness.
counterfactuals.output:
**Two Rooms, One Wall**

We were born from the same red weather,
split like lightning finds two paths down one tree—
you took the branch that faced the ocean,
I took the one that learned to count.

Somewhere our blood still remembers
being a single river before the fork,
before the map insisted on two names.

I keep a jar of your baby teeth
though I don't recall you giving them to me.
Maybe I stole them in the womb,
greedy for anything that proved we once
shared a heartbeat like a secret
neither of us asked to keep.

Now you call on years that aren't quite holidays,
your voice arriving like weather from another climate—
familiar rain, unfamiliar sky.
We talk about nothing
the way surgeons talk before an operation,
careful, precise, avoiding the wound
we both know is between us.

I dreamed we were two hands
that forgot they belonged to the same body,
reaching for the same falling glass
from opposite ends of a very long table.
Neither of us caught it.
We just watched the shine of it
break into a hundred small mirrors,
each one holding a different age we used to be.

Sometimes tenderness hides in the ordinary cruelty
of not-calling, not-asking, not-saying
the thing that would cost us
the architecture we've built to survive each other.

I know your sleep-sounds still,
though I haven't heard them in a decade.
I know the specific ache in your left shoulder
from the year we shared a bed
and a fear of the dark that had two separate names
but only one shadow.

If you cut me now,
would you bleed too?
Not from sympathy—
from the old contract blood makes with blood,
promising that no matter how far the branches drift,
the roots still tangle somewhere
underground, in the dark,
where neither of us has to admit
we are reaching for the same water.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a poem exploring intimacy and estrangement between two people who live close but avoid real contact, using metaphors of magic tricks and acrobatics.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Distance of Near Things

We share a house like two magicians
who've forgotten how to break the spell—
each morning, sawing ourselves in half
across the breakfast table, smiling
through the illusion, never quite
revealing where the body went.

You fold yourself into small boxes,
disappear behind the newspaper's curtain.
I applaud from habit, not surprise.
We've rehearsed this vanishing so long
the trick performs itself now,
hands moving without hearts attached.

I am a tightrope walker in our kitchen,
balancing the weight of unsaid things,
arms out for a partner who's already
climbed down from his side of the wire,
gone to practice solo somersaults
in some private, silent tent.

Once we caught each other—remember?—
trapeze artists trusting empty air,
your hands finding my wrists exactly
when the fall began. Now we juggle
separately, dropping words like torches
we're too tired to relight.

At night we sleep like sword-swallowers,
each throat closed around its private blade,
performing the astonishing feat
of proximity without touch,
of breathing the same recycled air
while living in completely different acts.

The audience has gone home years ago.
There's no one left to gasp or clap
when I walk through you like a ghost
in a cabinet trick gone wrong,
when you look through me
like the assistant in the box—

still smiling, still waving scarves,
still pretending there's a woman there
instead of just the space
where someone
used
to be.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a dense, imagistic poem about two hearts that beat in careful synchrony to avoid true vulnerability, blending domestic details with circus imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Careful Act

We keep the house like a tent half-struck—
teacups balanced on the edges of saucers,
your coat on its hook like a hung trapeze,
waiting for hands that never quite let go
of the safety bar.

I have learned the exact weight
of your silence at breakfast,
the way you fold newspaper corners
into small, precise mathematics.
I fold mine to match.
This is our act: two hearts
walking the same wire,
never touching,
each footfall timed to the other's breath
so neither of us falls
and neither of us flies.

In the ring of our kitchen,
the dog performs its small tricks for toast.
The kettle screams on cue.
We have rehearsed this so long
the danger looks like grace—
look how we lean, look how we don't,
two tightropes strung parallel
close enough to borrow warmth,
too far to feel the burn.

At night your hand finds mine
under blankets like a net
we've triple-checked, triple-knotted,
and still we sleep with one eye open,
still our hearts drum separate time signatures
disguised as harmony,
metronomes set just close enough
to sound, from a distance,
like a single pulse.

Somewhere under all this canvas
a lion could be sleeping
or empty air.
We never lift the tent flap far enough to see.
We just keep polishing the spangles,
keep the spotlight aimed
at the safe parts of the show—
the juggling, the doves,
the elephant who never remembers
what it means to be wild,
chained so long to the domestic stake
she's stopped testing the rope.

We call this love:
the sequined discipline of almost,
the practiced bow before an audience of none,
two hearts drumming in perfect time
to avoid the one, terrible rhythm
of being truly heard.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical piece about twins or doubles who share space but keep emotional distance, incorporating motifs of sleight of hand, magician's swords, and heartbeat rhythms.
counterfactuals.output:
# Two Chambers, One Door

We were cut from the same trick,
sawn in half and never quite
put back together right—
two halves that learned to walk apart
while sharing a single heart's
strange arithmetic: one beat, then
a pause where the other should be.

Watch closely. Watch my hands.
This is how we learned to live—
the misdirection perfected early,
the palming of small griefs,
the way I'd vanish a doubt
into my sleeve before you saw
it catch the light.

We sleep in the same house
like swords sheathed in a box,
parallel, gleaming, never touching,
each blade sharpened
against the absence of the other.
The assistant smiles. The blades slide home.
Nothing bleeds. That's the whole point—
to look pierced through
and still stand up applauding.

Ba-dum. Ba-dum.
Two rhythms trying to pass
as one sustained note,
syncopated by all
the things we do not say
across the dinner table,
across the hallway,
across the twelve-inch gap
between our beds
that might as well be
the velvet curtain,
might as well be
the cabinet door
swinging shut.

You are my nearest distance.
You are the card I know
is up my sleeve
but pretend to be surprised by.

We do this dance of proximity—
sharing walls, sharing blood,
sharing the choreography of avoidance
so well-rehearsed it looks like ease,
like closeness, like two doves
in the same box
who never once
lock eyes.

Somewhere below the trick,
below the swords and scarves,
two hearts insist on beating
in the same locked cabinet,
knocking faintly,
their small SOS
mistaken, night after night,
for applause.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft an abstract, metaphor-heavy poem about forbearance and restraint in a close relationship, using unusual physical and sensory imagery like walnut oil, fitted sheets, and rib cages.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Ribs Know

Consider the walnut oil—how it sits
in the dark cabinet of itself, patient,
not yet poured, not yet
the thing that makes the wood shine.
This is what I have become for you:
a held thing. An almost.

I fold the fitted sheet alone in the hallway,
that impossible origami of elastic corners,
and think how restraint is like this—
the way you must find the shape
before you can make it small,
must know the give
before you know the folding.

My rib cage is a house of doors
I keep deciding not to open.
Each breath a small negotiation
between the wanting and the wall.
You sleep three feet away
and I am counting archways,
I am counting all the rooms
I do not walk into.

There is a way of loving
that looks like water not spilled—
the glass carried steady
across a floor gone slippery
with all the things unsaid.
Walnut oil dark and viscous,
patient in its glass throat,
waiting for the exact
right grain of wood,
the exact moment
when pouring
becomes a kind of mercy
instead of a flood.

I have learned to hold my body
like a question I don't ask.
To let the fitted sheet
stay wrinkled at the edges,
a small imperfection
I choose over the alternative:
the version where I unmake
everything gentle
just to feel it move.

Some nights my ribs contract
like a fist that isn't hitting anything,
just closing, just practicing
the shape of not,
the muscle memory of stillness—
this is not absence. This is
architecture. This is the oil
still sealed, still amber,
still becoming
whatever waits
beyond the pour.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
